findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a series label rather than a hook, burying the actual hook in sentence two.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of GIT UNDO: THE FIELD MANUAL. \"I lost my commits with reset --hard\" is almost always false — the commits are still sitting in your reflog."
findings.fix: Lead with the hook and move the part label after it: "'I lost my commits with reset --hard' is almost always false — the commits are still sitting in your reflog. Part 2 of GIT UNDO: THE FIELD MANUAL walks every undo Git gives you: ..."
Run the fit pass — it adds material from the book without removing anything.

findings.summary: The recovery-window table claims `git gc --prune=now` destroys unreachable commits, but objects still referenced by unexpired reflog entries are reachable and survive that command.
findings.evidence: table row: ["After `gc --prune=now`","gone"] — but git-gc keeps objects referenced by reflogs; the documented sequence to actually destroy them is `git reflog expire --expire=now --all` followed by `git gc --prune=now`.
findings.fix: Change the row to `reflog expire --expire=now --all` + `gc --prune=now` → "gone", and if you keep a `gc --prune=now` row label it "only objects no reflog still points at". The note "plain `git gc` keeps reflog commits" should then say that any `gc` keeps them until the reflog entry itself expires (90 days reachable / 30 days unreachable).

findings.summary: The part's organizing decision rule appears fourth, after three sections of recovery trivia that only make sense once the reader knows which undo family they are in.
findings.evidence: Heading order on page 1 is "5. Three Things To Trust" → "6. Recovery Window" → "7. Cheap Insurance" → "8. One Question Decides It" → "9. Reset Depth Ladder".
findings.fix: Lead page 1 with "One Question Decides It" and the reset depth ladder (the routing map), then follow with Three Things To Trust, Recovery Window, and Cheap Insurance as the safety-net material.
Run the fit pass — it adds material from the book without removing anything.

findings.summary: Page 2 opens with an unlabelled reset code block whose examples belong to the depth-ladder table left behind on page 1.
findings.evidence: Page 2's first block is code with no preceding heading: "git reset --soft HEAD~3  # squash", "git reset HEAD app.js  # unstage", "git reset --hard @{u}  # = remote"; the matching heading "9. Reset Depth Ladder" and its `--soft`/`--mixed`/`--hard` table are the last blocks of page 1.
findings.fix: Move this code block onto page 1 directly beneath the "9. Reset Depth Ladder" table, or give it its own heading on page 2 (e.g. "9b. Reset In Practice").

findings.summary: The pin graphic on the section 7 sticky note sits on top of the code line and obscures the first letter of "untracked".
findings.evidence: Code line reads "git stash -u  # park everything, untracked too" but the pin overlaps the word so it renders as "...everything, ␣ntracked too".
findings.fix: Move the sticky note and its pin down/right so the pin anchor clears the last code line's bounding box in the Cheap Insurance block.

findings.summary: The stash-recovery claim on page 1 is asserted with no supporting command; the example that proves it only arrives on page 2.
findings.evidence: Page 1: "Stash is commits in disguise — fsck finds it after a drop"; the supporting lines "git fsck --unreachable | grep commit" and "git stash apply <sha>" appear only in page 2's section 11.
findings.fix: Either attach the two-command recovery snippet to the page 1 bullet, or reword the bullet to forward-reference it ("— recoverable after a drop; see §11").

findings.summary: The recovery window table states two different survival periods without telling the learner which one applies to their situation.
findings.evidence: Rows read "Unreachable, via reflog | ~30 days" and "Prune grace period | 2 weeks", with no rule connecting them.
findings.fix: Add a qualifier — e.g. change the second row to "No reflog entry (fresh clone, expired) | 2 weeks" — so each row names the condition under which its window governs.

findings.summary: The gc note is attached to the backup-command block it does not describe, instead of the recovery-window table it qualifies.
findings.evidence: Section 7's code is "git branch backup-$(date +%s)" / "git stash -u", and its note reads "plain `git gc` keeps reflog commits" — while section 6's table row "After `gc --prune=now` | gone" carries no such note.
findings.fix: Move "plain `git gc` keeps reflog commits" to a note under the section 6 Recovery Window table.

findings.summary: The takeaway calls never-added working-tree changes "the only point of no return", contradicting the page-1 table where committed work is also permanently gone after reflog expiry/pruning.
findings.evidence: "Everything Git tracks is recoverable except working-tree changes that were never added and never committed. That is the only point of no return." vs. page 1: ["Unreachable, via reflog","~30 days"] / ["After `gc --prune=now`","gone"]
findings.fix: Qualify it: "Inside the reflog window, everything Git has ever recorded is recoverable; the only thing never recoverable is working-tree content that was never added and never committed — and even recorded work goes away once the reflog expires and objects are pruned."

findings.summary: The pin on the "--hard destroys uncommitted work" note overlaps the third code line between the comment marker and its text.
findings.evidence: Line 3 renders as "git reset --hard @{u}  #  = remote" with the pin covering the gap after "#".
findings.fix: Shift the sticky note/pin below the code block's last line so it does not overlay "# = remote".

findings.summary: The pin on the "inspect with git show before resetting" note overlaps the final code line in section 11, partially covering "dropped".
findings.evidence: Line reads "git stash apply <sha>  # dropped stash" with the pin drawn over the "pp" of "dropped".
findings.fix: Lower the note/pin anchor so it starts below the last code line of the Undo The Undo block.

findings.summary: The unstage example uses the legacy spelling that contradicts the recommendation given two sections earlier, with no note that they are equivalent.
findings.evidence: Page 1 section 8 says "Staged → `git restore --staged <path>`"; page 2's code says "git reset HEAD app.js  # unstage".
findings.fix: Change the comment to `# unstage (= git restore --staged)` or swap the line for `git reset --mixed HEAD~1  # un-commit, keep edits` so the reset block stops re-teaching a job already assigned to `restore`.

findings.summary: The `@{u}` revision shorthand is used before it is defined, and its inline gloss is inaccurate.
findings.evidence: "git reset --hard @{u}  # = remote" — `@{u}` appears nowhere else in the part, and `@{n}`-style notation is only introduced later via "git reset --hard HEAD@{1}".
findings.fix: Expand the comment to `# @{u} = upstream, e.g. origin/main` or write the branch out as `git reset --hard origin/main`.
